title: Stopping host should detect when instance is stopped without depending on timing
description: [This piece of code|https://github.com/evergreen-ci/evergreen/blob/f8d313109ff81e1413df35455dad402a7aa674a2/cloud/ec2.go#L944-L975] attempts to stop the host but does not do so in an idempotent way. If the check for host status fails (which is not guaranteed to succeed since it depends on how long the host takes to shut down), the host will be stuck in the stopping state with no way to recover. We should check if the host is stopped every time this is called and not just blindly make an AWS call which may fail. We also should unset the stopping state and revert to the old state if it fails. This code should not rely on sleeping as a reliabl mechanism to try to give the host time to shut down.

This code should not rely on sleeping as a reliabl mechanism to try to give the host time to shut down.

In that case, we should always fall back to returning the response body as the error text if a gimlet response can't be parsed.

title: Allow passing a YAML document to host.create
description: As part of PM-1822, the STM team would like to dramatically simplify the process for authoring and running performance workloads. A significant part of the work involves simplifying how the infrastructure is provisioned. The status quo has been to use {{terraform}}, which can be configured through YAML files. See [example config here|https://github.com/10gen/dsi/blob/master/configurations/infrastructure_provisioning/infrastructure_provisioning.M60-like-replica.yml]. There are a few pain points with this approach    1. users need to go through mana to add their ssh credentials and configure DSI to use them  2. we're limited to a single az without a significant refactor  3. we can't enforce the life cycle of the spawned hosts without outside help (e.g. ec2-reaper)  4. terraform doesn't always successfully teardown all components in the cluster, e.g. security groups.    These are all problems that Evergreen has solved. So it makes sense logically for Evergreen to handle the topology of performance tasks. In fact, {{host.create}} already does this.    The one caveat is that terraform allows topologies to be created locally in an identical manner to an Evergreen task, which {{host.create}} currently cannot do. For adding performance tests and triaging problems, it's a common use case to run a portion of a test, tweak some knobs, then rerun the test, which is hard to do in a patch build and is similar to what spawn hosts are frequently used for.    For performance tests, we need to be able to spin up hosts with a particular distro, az, network interface options (which is usually the default), and optionally the EC2 region. Each cluster will contain hosts with different distros and AZs.    In order to migrate DSI to host.create, it would be nice to have a single mechanism to spin up hosts in Evergreen and locally using an interface similar to that of {{host.create}}. I'd also be happy to discuss an alternative interface where Evergreen has more knowledge of the topology require less configuration than what's currently exposed in {{host.create}}, otherwise this logic can live in DSI.    See linked TIG tickets for more info on use cases

title: Allow processes to close their resources gracefully and reconsider sharing connections between remote clients and processes
description: The close method would help with cleaning up resources because the SSH library has to open an SSH session, which should be gracefully shut down. The only resource we really need to stop in the local is the transition/reactor goroutines in basic/blocking process to ensure the executor is closed. title: Scoped jobs that are undispatchable should have scopes removed or be deleted
description: It seems like barque still has problems with re-dispatching old jobs with scopes that exceed the lock timeout. One possible reason is that jobs with a {{DispatchBy}} requirement may not be able to run if too long has passed, so they will be stuck unable to dispatch and also will not clear their scopes. For jobs that have scopes and are stuck in progress but can't be re-dispatched due to {{DispatchBy}}, we should just unset their scopes and mark them complete.

title: Don't Log IDE panics
description: [reverse_proxy|https://github.com/golang/go/blob/cc8838d645b2b7026c1f3aaceb011775c5ca3a08/src/net/http/httputil/reverseproxy.go#L299] sometimes panics if there's an error while streaming the response back to the client (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/23643).  Our [middleware|https://github.com/evergreen-ci/gimlet/blob/185166ff85e8801545747fa65a14486e0fe4680b/middleware_grip.go#L166] recovers the panic and logs to slack. Because the panic isn't actionable we need to log at a lower level.    One design is to recover the panic in the route so it doesn't make it all the way back up to the recovery logger.
clean_text: Don't Log IDE panics. reverse_proxy sometimes panics if there's an error while streaming the response back to the client (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/23643). These are common points of confusion for users, so we should provide a quick fix to mitigate the confusion until we arrive at a long-term solution in EVG-13201.    Per a discussion with DAG, it's not feasible to only surface execution tasks to users, since DAG tooling relies heavily on display tasks. In light of issues like EVG-12591, Spruce should not allow restarting of individual execution tasks in this short term solution. The recent completion of EVG-5856 gives a predictable place for users to input/execute these scripts. The request in this ticket is to better utilize that box with a set of predefined (in configuration...somewhere) project options in an effort to make these scripts trivially discoverable for newcomers..    For example, server engineers are often spawning hosts from task failures with core dumps to inspect their contents. However finding the core dumps and properly setting up gdb are still mostly trial and error for the uninitiated. The initiated have [published|https://wiki.corp.mongodb.com/display/~<USER>Unarchive+required+files+to+gdb+analyze+coredump+on+spawnhost] scripts [on the interwebs|https://gist.github.com/GWlodarek/681006048f51f3e8195517c00860dfd4] and [other|https://wiki.corp.mongodb.com/display/WT/Troubleshooting+Test+Failures] webpages [link to|https://wiki.corp.mongodb.com/display/WT/Symbolising+mongod+callstack+in+BFs] those [resources|https://wiki.corp.mongodb.com/display/~<USER>Stuff+I+always+forget+how+to+do]. Having these scripts available on the wiki or as gists still leaves them rather undiscoverable.     This ask would also close the remaining feature gap requested in EVG-7484 and probably EVG-7477.

title: Spruce displays execution tasks intended to be restarted as system failures
description: Spruce separates display tasks into individual execution tasks in the [patch details|https://spruce.mongodb.com/version/5f43f081d6d80a3602a3c14f/tasks?page=0&taskName=burn_in] view. In contrast, the legacy UI only exposes execution tasks through their [display task|https://evergreen.mongodb.com/task/mongodb_mongo_v4.4_enterprise_rhel_62_64_bit_inmem_required_display_burn_in_tests_patch_29e21d0ff597e6dd10bbb9bab4086612339443ca_5f43f081d6d80a3602a3c14f_20_08_24_16_53_31##comparehashes=29e21d0ff597e6dd10bbb9bab4086612339443ca&threads=all].    When a display task encounters a system failure due to an AWS host being terminated, Evergreen will restart it, rather than mark the task as a system failure. In Spruce, because the execution tasks are broken out, they will appear as failed with a system failure in this case. This implies that there's action required from the user to address the system failure, when in reality the task will restart and the failure should resolve on its own.    A potential solution to address this is to display these 'system failed' execution tasks as 'in progress', since for all intents and purposes the task has not yet completed. The task details page can provide further information on whether a task is truly in progress or slated to be restarted, for users interested in differentiating between those two states.

title: Auto-restart display tasks even if there are blocked execution tasks
description: Presently, if an execution task encounters a system failure due to a terminated AWS host, its parent display task will attempt to restart, unless the display task has blocked execution tasks.   In the blocked execution tasks case, a user would need to manually restart the display task in order to recover from the AWS host termination.  We should consider auto-restarting display tasks in this case as well.    One potential confusion with the auto-restart is the following scenario. A display task with blocked execution tasks is auto-restarted. Prior to the restart, some execution tasks failed with system failures and other tasks didn't run at all, being blocked. The display task is restarted and all tasks complete successfully. The confusion is that the tasks that had been blocked would have results from multiple executions, while only having truly executed once. Ideally, once EVG-12897 is complete, most users would not need to refer to the multiple executions, since the system failures would no longer be surfaced.

sys-perf patch, I significantly increased the buffering of events and amount of concurrency when streaming events to poplar grpc. The throughput of the operations wasn't calculated in the perf ui, and there are some negative durations.    Looking at the generated .ftdc files, the timestamps are out of order, while the cedar calculation of wallclock duration seems to be using the [first and last element listed|https://github.com/evergreen-ci/cedar/blob/e3c5d337c2c8ff346c09d5db95515ab4657d367c/perf/ftdc_rollups.go#L81]. I think the increase concurrency and buffering may be causing us to send them to poplar in different orders. Grpc only guarantees an ordering to events within a single stream, whereas we have many.    I think a straightforward solution would be to use the min/max timestamps instead of the first and last elements, but I'm not sure if poplar is _supposed_ to be guaranteeing a timestamp order when writing to disk, or if there are any other implications of the elements being out of order to deal with.

Looking at the generated .ftdc files, the timestamps are out of order, while the cedar calculation of wallclock duration seems to be using the first and last element listed. I think the increase concurrency and buffering may be causing us to send them to poplar in different orders. Grpc only guarantees an ordering to events within a single stream, whereas we have many. title: take generated tasks into account when generating slowdowns for post hoc task analysis
description: display_version_slowdown currently does not correctly take into account the implicit dependency in task generation. It only looks at depends_on. display_only tasks are said to depend_on the tasks that the tasks they generate depend on, but can start well before these tasks. This leads to instances, such as mongodb_mongo_master_fbafa599da8f316e508d0a152586a77e85805c29 , where the slowdown is less than zero. Additionally, The topological ordering of the task DAG implicitly treats generated tasks as equivalent in start time to tasks scheduled at the very beginning. This could lead to an underestimate, rather than overestimate, of idealized runtime. I think the following approach will correct this:    Remove dependencies of display_only tasks.    Create a dummy """"generator node"""", whose end time is equivalent to the time of the generated task's creation, whose start time is equivalent to the generator task's start time, and which ¿depends on the same tasks as the generator task, if genuine dependencies can be found?  depends on. This embeds the dependency implied by ordering of task scheduling/creation time into the structure of the graph.

title: Handle custom builds when downloading binaries on hosts from S3
description: Staging will not download binaries from S3, but production will (to reduce load on the server during deploys). In order for production to download from S3, the binaries must have been uploaded to the desired location in S3 or else binary downloads will fail. Because custom builds may or may not have uploaded the binaries to the S3 location, we have to come up with a way to do one of the following:   # Disable downloading binaries from S3 (so that it downloads from the app server). I'm assuming that people will _not_ remember  (or know) to disable the admin setting flag for downloading from S3 (EVG-13258) when deploying a custom build to production.   # Guarantee that the binaries are uploaded in the correct location in S3.    There's several options to deal with this, with some options such as:   * Add a large warning text when someone deploys a custom build to production (easy, but you still have to see the text in the output).   * As a pre-deploy step, require that the binaries in dist.tar.gz be uploaded to S3 before deploying the custom build. This would slow down custom build deploys, but would allow the binaries to be downloaded from S3 and would not require any database changes (slowest option, but would require no code changes to deal with it in the application code).   * When deploying a custom build, disable the database feature flag for using S3 URLs vs. app server URLs to download binaries.   * Modify host provisioning to try downloading the binary from S3 first, and download from the app server as a fallback. If it fails to download from S3 (due to 403/404), fall back to downloading it from the app server. This could be a bit wasteful in provisioning time, but assuming custom build deploys are uncommon, it might not be that bad in terms of performance.

Because custom builds may or may not have uploaded the binaries to the S3 location, we have to come up with a way to do one of the following: # Disable downloading binaries from S3 (so that it downloads from the app server). I'm assuming that people will _not_ remember (or know) to disable the admin setting flag for downloading from S3 (EVG-13258) when deploying a custom build to production. # Guarantee that the binaries are uploaded in the correct location in S3. There's several options to deal with this, with some options such as: * Add a large warning text when someone deploys a custom build to production (easy, but you still have to see the text in the output). * As a pre-deploy step, require that the binaries in dist.tar.gz be uploaded to S3 before deploying the custom build. This would slow down custom build deploys, but would allow the binaries to be downloaded from S3 and would not require any database changes (slowest option, but would require no code changes to deal with it in the application code). * When deploying a custom build, disable the database feature flag for using S3 URLs vs. app server URLs to download binaries. * Modify host provisioning to try downloading the binary from S3 first, and download from the app server as a fallback. If it fails to download from S3 (due to 403/404), fall back to downloading it from the app server. This could be a bit wasteful in provisioning time, but assuming custom build deploys are uncommon, it might not be that bad in terms of performance.
